task.goal: Help a repair shop give accurate pickup estimates when parts arrival varies.
hard_constraints: Two staff, paper job cards and an existing supplier email inbox; no paid software.
Do not promise a date unsupported by parts status or hide delays.
Compare missed estimates, customer calls and staff time for four weeks.
task.available_resources: Past 30 job records and supplier replies.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Parts-status gates with a firm next-update commitment
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Replace a single pickup date with explicit evidence gates on each paper job card: ordered with no confirmed dispatch; dispatched with supplier arrival range; physically received and checked; repair scheduled. The mechanism is to prevent uncertain supply information from becoming a customer promise while giving customers a reliable time to hear next.

One staff member checks supplier email at two fixed times daily and records the latest status, its timestamp and the next check on affected cards. The other uses that entry when speaking to customers; both can cover either role. Before receipt, say, for example: “The supplier reports arrival Tuesday–Thursday. Pickup is still unconfirmed; we will update you Wednesday afternoon.” Offer a conditional pickup window only when supplier evidence and available repair capacity support it, stating those conditions. Once the correct parts are received and checked, assign a pickup window against the shop’s actual workload. Notify customers promptly when evidence invalidates a previously communicated window, explaining the cause and revised status.

Use the 30 past records to identify common unsupported promises and estimate ordinary repair time after parts receipt. Implementation requires only a handwritten status key, job-card fields, the existing inbox and a daily callback list. It assumes staff can reliably connect supplier replies to jobs and reserve realistic workshop capacity. It cannot make unreliable supplier information accurate; its benefit may primarily be fewer premature promises and fewer uncertainty-driven calls. Customers needing a date immediately may find the process less satisfying.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Run for four weeks, alternating new eligible jobs between this process and current practice, with both groups receiving honest delay disclosures. Use the past 30 records as context where timestamps exist, not as a complete baseline by assumption. On paper, tally missed communicated pickup dates/windows, inbound status calls and staff minutes for checks, updates and calls; record how many jobs received any pickup estimate and how early. Inspect unresolved jobs at week four separately. The mechanism is challenged if supported estimates still miss as often, calls do not fall, or communication time rises without improved reliability. Check that apparent gains are not solely due to withholding every estimate.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Evidence-based conditional ranges from comparable past jobs
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use the shop’s own supply history to express uncertainty as a conditional range rather than treating a supplier’s expected arrival as a certain pickup date. The mechanism is calibration: estimates reflect observed variation for comparable parts orders and include the shop’s remaining repair workload.

Review the 30 job records alongside supplier replies. Where dates are available, write down order, dispatch, receipt and ready-for-pickup dates. Group only genuinely comparable jobs, such as the same supplier and stock status; avoid creating many tiny categories. On a paper reference sheet, show the observed delivery span and the number of examples behind it. Do not describe that span as a guaranteed bound or a statistically established confidence interval. Sparse or inconsistent groups receive “insufficient evidence for a pickup window.”

For each new job, record the supplier’s current evidence and use relevant historical variation as a reasonableness check. Give a conditional pickup range only if the current supplier status, comparable history and workshop capacity support one: “If the dispatched part arrives within the supplier’s range, we expect collection Thursday–Monday; this remains provisional until it arrives.” If supplier evidence conflicts with history, investigate and explain the uncertainty rather than averaging it away. Review affected cards daily and contact customers when the range changes or becomes unsupported. Confirm pickup after parts inspection and scheduling.

One staff member maintains the reference sheet and inbox annotations; the other records communicated ranges and revisions on job cards. This needs no software beyond the inbox. It assumes useful dates and some comparable past jobs exist. Thirty records may be too few, and changing supplier conditions can invalidate historical patterns. In those cases, communicate status and the next update time instead of inventing precision.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For four weeks, alternate eligible jobs between these conditional ranges and the shop’s current honest estimating practice. Log initial and revised windows, misses against the initial window, inbound status calls and total staff minutes. Track window width, lead time and jobs without estimates so broad or late ranges cannot masquerade as better accuracy. Use the historical sheet only where supporting examples are visible. A small falsifying check is whether comparable deliveries immediately fall outside its observed span repeatedly; suspend that grouping if so. Judge the process unsuccessful if misses remain comparable while windows become substantially less useful or staff time increases.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Exception-triggered supplier clarification and delay recovery
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make pickup estimates more accurate by resolving missing or contradictory parts information before it contaminates the estimate. The primary mechanism is targeted exception handling: staff pursue the few supply uncertainties threatening customer commitments instead of treating all supplier replies as equally informative.

Use the 30 past jobs and supplier replies to identify recurring warning signs, such as an order acknowledgement mistaken for dispatch, a backorder without a replenishment date, or an expected arrival passing without tracking movement. These are investigation triggers, not proof that a delivery will fail. On each paper job card, record the current supplier evidence, any supported conditional pickup window, the next supply milestone and the latest time that milestone can occur without undermining that window. Include repair time and workshop capacity when setting that threshold.

At one daily inbox review, one staff member pulls cards whose milestone is missing, overdue or contradictory. Using the existing supplier email channel, ask a specific question: Is this allocated stock? Has it dispatched? What arrival range is currently supported? Request a tracking reference where applicable. If a supported alternative part or delivery option is available, assess compatibility, cost and customer authorization before changing the order; the process does not depend on alternatives existing. The second staff member contacts affected customers as soon as their current window loses support, even if the supplier has not replied. State what changed, what is unknown and when the next update will come. Never retain an invalid window while awaiting clarification.

Implementation needs a handwritten exception list, short email templates and clear daily ownership. It assumes suppliers sometimes provide useful clarification and staff can identify milestone dependencies. Supplier silence, missing records or universal backorders may leave accuracy unchanged; escalation still cannot justify an unsupported date.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Trial for four weeks, alternating new jobs between exception handling and current practice, with equal requirements to disclose known delays. Compare missed initial pickup estimates, inbound customer status calls and staff minutes, including supplier chasing. Record estimate availability, revisions and unresolved jobs. For each trigger, note whether clarification arrived before the threatened window and whether it materially changed the estimate or repair plan. The mechanism is weakened if chasing mostly produces no actionable information, warnings arrive too late, or misses and calls remain unchanged while staff time rises. Inspect several triggered cards against their emails to verify that revised promises have actual evidence.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A protected repair slot for jobs released by arriving parts
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Reduce pickup uncertainty by protecting workshop capacity for jobs whose parts arrive unexpectedly. The mechanism is operational: shorten and stabilize the wait between parts receipt and repair completion, so variable deliveries do not also create an unpredictable workshop queue.

Review the 30 past job cards and supplier replies for any recorded gap between parts receipt and repair start. If that gap is substantial, trial one small, protected repair block on working days. Size it using documented repair durations and the two staff members’ available hours; do not assume historical timestamps exist. Fill the rest of the schedule normally. Until a stated daily cutoff, keep the protected block available for the oldest waiting job whose complete, correct parts have arrived and whose remaining work fits. If none qualifies, release it to ordinary work. Longer repairs require separately available capacity.

Use a paper diary alongside the job cards. One staff member checks arrivals and records remaining work; the other assigns the block and communicates the resulting pickup estimate. Both can cover either role. Before parts arrive, explain that pickup remains unconfirmed and give a next-update time. After receipt and inspection, estimate pickup from an actual available block and a credible repair duration. Record and disclose delays immediately if diagnosis changes or the block becomes unavailable.

This requires no purchased tools, but it consumes scheduling flexibility and may delay other work. It assumes staff control the schedule, enough repairs fit the block, and waiting after receipt is a meaningful source of error. It will offer little benefit where supplier transit dominates the entire delay or every repair requires lengthy, unpredictable work.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare two weeks of current scheduling with two weeks using protected blocks, keeping truthful status updates throughout. On paper, record missed original pickup estimates, inbound status calls and staff minutes spent scheduling, checking and communicating. Also record receipt-to-start time, completed jobs, unused block minutes and estimate availability. Report unfinished jobs separately. Inspect the first five eligible arrivals: if the protected block seldom advances their start, the mechanism lacks support. Four-week differences remain tentative because job mix and deliveries may change; reject the approach if it merely transfers delays to other customers without improving estimate reliability.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Check the whole repair requirement before estimating pickup
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Reduce estimate failures caused by discovering an additional required part after the initially ordered part arrives. The mechanism is an early completeness check: establish which parts and diagnostic dependencies must be resolved for the whole repair, then base the estimate on the slowest unresolved requirement. This could help when individually accurate supplier arrival information still produces inaccurate pickup estimates because the original parts list was incomplete.

Review the 30 past job records and supplier replies for documented additional orders, incompatible parts or repairs that required further diagnosis after dismantling. Use those examples to create a short handwritten checklist for recurring repair types; missing documentation is not evidence that these problems never occurred.

Before ordering, the diagnosing staff member lists required parts, compatibility details and any checks that could reveal further requirements. The second staff member briefly checks that list against the diagnosis and proposed order. Perform only practical, authorized inspections; record dependencies that cannot yet be resolved. On the paper job card, give each required item its own supplier status and mark the requirement that currently controls completion.

Explain unresolved dependencies to the customer. If an inspection must wait until the first part arrives, say that pickup cannot yet be estimated reliably and commit to an update. Offer a pickup window only when the complete repair requirements, supplier evidence and available workshop time support it. Communicate newly discovered requirements and resulting delays promptly.

This needs a checklist, a few extra job-card fields and time from both staff, using the existing inbox. It assumes incomplete diagnosis or ordering contributes to delays and that some omissions are detectable beforehand. It offers little benefit when requirements are already consistently complete or delivery variation alone causes misses.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
For four weeks, alternate new eligible jobs between the completeness check and ordinary diagnosis and ordering, with both groups disclosing uncertainties and delays honestly. Record misses against the first communicated pickup window, inbound customer status calls and total staff minutes, including inspection, checking, supplier correspondence and customer updates. Also record additional orders discovered after the initial order, estimate availability and unfinished jobs.

Inspect the first five checked jobs: did the review identify a necessary item or unresolved dependency that ordinary preparation had missed? Compare subsequent additional-order delays across groups. The mechanism lacks support if checks uncover no useful omissions and additional-order delays remain similar while staff time increases. Treat four-week differences as tentative if volumes are small; do not count withholding all estimates as improved accuracy.

EXPAND.title: Reserve repair capacity against uncertain arrivals
EXPAND.proposal:
Make a supported pickup estimate more dependable by protecting the repair time it requires. Variable parts arrivals can bunch several jobs into the same day; accurate delivery information alone does not prevent the resulting workshop queue.

One staff member reviews the 30 job records for usable evidence of repair time after parts receipt and interruptions caused by arriving work. Both staff then maintain a paper capacity ledger beside the job cards. List available repair blocks, existing commitments and a small allowance for interruptions. Choose the allowance from available records and staff experience, marking it provisional where evidence is weak.

For a job with a supplier-supported arrival range, provisionally reserve sufficient repair time after the late end of that range. Communicate a conditional pickup window only if that reservation and the parts evidence support it. If delivery remains unknown, communicate status and a next-update time without reserving an indefinite sequence of blocks. On receipt, check the parts and convert the reservation into a firm work allocation. Release unused blocks promptly. If arrival slips beyond its reservation, notify the customer and allocate the next feasible block before issuing another estimate.

This differs from simply considering current workload: the ledger prevents subsequent bookings from consuming capacity already underpinning an estimate. It requires only paper, the existing inbox and consistent booking discipline. It assumes repair durations are reasonably estimable. Unexpected faults and clustered late deliveries can still defeat reservations; excessive protection can leave staff idle or lengthen quoted waits.
EXPAND.experiment:
For four weeks, the staff member responsible for bookings owns the ledger. Compare with a simple parts-status gate process that checks current workload but does not reserve future blocks. Alternate booking days between the two methods, honor every existing reservation and mark cross-group interference because both methods share capacity.

Record missed original pickup windows, inbound status calls and staff minutes, including ledger maintenance. Also record estimate availability, quoted waiting time, completed jobs and idle blocks attributable to reservations. Inspect the first five receipts to see whether reserved capacity actually prevented displacement. Stop adding reservations if they repeatedly leave usable capacity idle while other work waits, without reducing capacity-caused misses. A small, shared-workshop trial may establish feasibility rather than a reliable causal effect.

EXPAND.title: Verify the complete parts kit before placing the order
EXPAND.proposal:
Prevent avoidable arrival uncertainty caused by ordering the wrong part, overlooking a required item or confusing a partial shipment with a complete repair kit. The mechanism changes the order itself before supplier timing becomes the main constraint.

Review the 30 job records and supplier replies for identifiable corrections, returns, supplementary orders and split shipments. Do not assume these occurred where the records are silent. Use any recurring examples to create a short handwritten ordering check: equipment identity, required specification, quantity, compatibility evidence and all parts known to be necessary for the planned repair.

The diagnosing staff member writes this information on the job card. Before the order is sent, the other staff member checks it against the equipment details and proposed repair. Resolve discrepancies first; if compatibility remains uncertain, ask the supplier through the existing inbox and tell the customer that pickup timing is unconfirmed. Necessary customer authorization must precede any changed scope or cost.

When the supplier replies, record each required item separately, including any split shipment. A supported pickup window must depend on the last necessary item and available repair capacity. On receipt, match the actual kit to the card before confirming timing. If inspection reveals a wrong or missing item, contact the supplier and customer promptly and withdraw any estimate that has lost support.

Unlike parts-status gates, this process aims to remove preventable extra ordering cycles. It needs two brief staff checks and paper fields, with no purchased tools. It assumes the initial diagnosis can identify the required kit. Hidden faults, uncertain compatibility and supplier packing errors remain possible; staff must not imply that verification eliminates them.
EXPAND.experiment:
The staff member who sends orders owns a four-week trial. Alternate eligible orders between this verification process and a simple parts-status gate process; both use honest estimates and prompt delay disclosure. Record missed original estimates, customer status calls and staff minutes, including checking, clarification and reordering. Also tally wrong or omitted items, supplementary orders, time to place an order and jobs receiving an estimate.

Inspect the first five checked orders against their receipts. The direct falsifying question is whether checking prevents or catches consequential discrepancies before ordering. Stop the universal second-person check if it repeatedly delays clean orders without finding actionable discrepancies; retain only checks supported by observed problems. With few discrepancies or incomplete historical records, four weeks may show no measurable advantage over status gates.

EXPAND.title: Use customer read-back to prevent provisional timing becoming a promise
EXPAND.proposal:
Reduce missed expectations caused when a customer hears a supplier arrival date as a pickup commitment, or remembers a provisional window after its conditions have changed. The mechanism is explicit confirmation of shared understanding, rather than better delivery forecasting.

First, review the available records and supplier replies for wording that mixes delivery, repair completion and collection. Missing conversation records cannot establish what customers understood. Prepare a short paper script separating three facts: the evidenced parts status, any supported pickup estimate with its condition, and the next time the shop will provide an update.

The staff member speaking to the customer records those facts on the job card and asks a brief, neutral read-back: “So we know we explained it clearly, what timing are you planning around?” If the customer repeats an unsupported date, clarify immediately and record the corrected understanding. Do not use agreement as evidence that the supplier will deliver. If the customer needs certainty the shop cannot support, say that pickup remains unconfirmed and agree a next-update time.

At handoff, the other staff member uses the same recorded statement. When evidence changes, contact the customer promptly, explicitly identify which previous estimate has changed, explain the current status and repeat the understanding check. If contact fails, record attempts and keep the card visibly flagged for follow-up; a sent message does not prove understanding.

This adds a feedback loop to the strongest relevant prior route, parts-status gates, which can still fail if accurate wording is misunderstood. It requires only job-card space and short conversations. Its limits include language barriers, customers feeling tested and added call time. Staff should take responsibility for clarity and accept a customer's preference to end the conversation.
EXPAND.experiment:
For four weeks, one staff member owns a paper comparison log. Alternate new jobs between parts-status gates with and without read-back, keeping the evidence requirements and update schedule identical. Record missed original shop estimates, inbound status calls and total staff minutes. Separately record spontaneous read-back discrepancies and later complaints about a different expected date; do not count improved understanding as improved actual completion accuracy.

Inspect the first five read-backs for substantive corrections. Stop routine read-back if customers repeatedly object or it adds time without uncovering misunderstandings; continue clear status communication. The process offers no demonstrated improvement if calls and expectation disputes remain similar after accounting for added minutes, even if staff report greater confidence.

EXPAND.title: Parts-status gates with accountable customer-update recovery
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade the parts-status gate route, the strongest direct fit for preventing unsupported pickup promises. Preserve its evidence gates, twice-daily supplier inbox checks, workload check and prompt disclosure of invalidated estimates. Add explicit responsibility for completing customer updates: the staff member who identifies a changed estimate owns the update until the other staff member accepts it on the paper job card. An interruption or an unanswered call does not discharge that responsibility.

Each card records supplier evidence and timestamp, the communicated pickup window and conditions, the next update due, and its owner. Before parts receipt, give a conditional window only when supplier evidence and repair capacity support it; otherwise give status and a next-update time. After receipt and inspection, allocate repair time before confirming pickup.

The changed action closes a recovery gap: if contact fails, mark the previous estimate as withdrawn internally, record the attempt and retain the card on the owner's pending list. Retry at the next twice-daily review or the customer's agreed contact time. If the owner becomes unavailable, the remaining staff member takes the pending list at that review. Never assume that attempted contact means the customer knows about the delay. At the next successful contact, explicitly correct the earlier estimate.

This needs only the two staff, paper cards and existing inbox. It assumes customers can usually be reached through their existing contact arrangements. It may reduce stale promises surviving interruptions, but cannot improve supplier reliability or guarantee successful contact. Compared with ordinary status gates, it adds a small tracking burden and potentially repeated contact attempts.
EXPAND.experiment:
One staff member owns a four-week paper comparison, alternating new jobs between ordinary status gates and this ownership-and-recovery version. Both groups must receive honest estimates and delay disclosures. Review the 30 past records and supplier replies for examples of changed estimates, without inferring undocumented contact failures.

Record misses against the original communicated pickup window, inbound customer status calls and total staff minutes, including failed contact attempts. Also record estimate availability, lead time, overdue updates and jobs unresolved at four weeks. Inspect the first five changed-estimate cards: does each have an owner, evidence and either completed contact or a pending recovery action? If none naturally encounters interruption, walk through one interrupted handoff on paper.

If recovery work causes updates to other customers to become overdue at two consecutive daily reviews, stop transferring updates between staff and use one daily owner with the other covering absence. Retain the evidence gates and delay disclosure. The added procedure earns its burden only if fewer updates are lost or calls fall without simply issuing fewer estimates; this small trial cannot establish a precise effect.

EXPAND.title: Repair reservations with an overrun response that protects later estimates
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade the capacity-reservation route, a competitive mechanism because variable deliveries can create a repair queue even when supplier information is accurate. Preserve the paper ledger, provisional repair blocks after the supported arrival range, parts inspection, prompt release of unused blocks and reallocation after late delivery. Add an explicit response when work already underway threatens the capacity promised to later customers.

Use usable portions of the 30 records to estimate repair durations, marking uncertain jobs clearly. One staff member owns the ledger for the day; both record interruptions and remaining work. Give a conditional pickup window only when the parts evidence and an actual reserved block support it. Unknown arrival dates receive status and a next-update time.

The changed action occurs when new faults or slower progress make an allocated block insufficient. The person doing the repair immediately tells the ledger owner and records the remaining work. Before adding another pickup commitment, the owner checks which existing windows still fit. Preserve existing reservations where feasible, use genuinely uncommitted time, and promptly revise any window that has lost support. Do not silently push all later reservations back. Additional repair scope or cost still requires the customer's ordinary authorization. While that authorization is pending, release capacity that can safely be used for other work; do not assume the interrupted repair can be resumed instantly.

This needs paper and brief staff coordination, and assumes repair progress can be assessed well enough to identify a meaningful overrun. Compared with the original ledger, it makes recovery from consumed capacity explicit, at the cost of reassessment and potentially earlier bad news. It cannot prevent hidden faults or create extra workshop capacity.
EXPAND.experiment:
The daily ledger owner runs a four-week comparison with the original reservation process, introducing the overrun response after two weeks. Honor all existing reservations throughout; the shared queue and changing job mix limit causal interpretation. Use past records only to inform initial duration allowances.

For both periods, tally missed original pickup windows, inbound status calls and total staff minutes. Also record estimate availability, quoted waits, completed jobs, idle reserved time and how many later commitments each overrun affected. Inspect the first actual overrun to see whether the owner made a feasible allocation and contacted affected customers before their windows expired. If no overrun occurs, use one past job for a paper walkthrough and report that the live mechanism remained untested.

If repeated reassessment takes more than ten minutes per day on three days without changing an allocation or customer update, stop the repeated reviews and perform one review when an overrun is first identified, then review again only when evidence changes. Retain prompt delay disclosure. Judge any reduction in misses alongside longer quoted waits and displaced work, rather than treating those costs as free.

EXPAND.title: Send complete orders at authorization to avoid losing supplier dispatch cycles
EXPAND.proposal:
Use order-release timing as a distinct mechanism: reduce avoidable waiting before the supplier can dispatch, rather than improve forecasting after an order is placed. The route tests whether batching orders until a later inbox session is an unnecessary dependency.

First, inspect the 30 job records and supplier replies for authorization, order-sent and dispatch timestamps, plus any explicit supplier cutoff or collection schedule. Do not infer a cutoff from a few coincidental dispatch times. Adopt this route only if there is evidence of shop-controlled order delay that could plausibly lose a dispatch opportunity. If records cannot establish that, keep current ordering and record those timestamps prospectively instead of claiming a benefit.

At the existing customer authorization conversation, the staff member handling the job checks that the diagnosis, required part and authorized cost are sufficiently settled to order. If they are, that staff member sends the order through the existing inbox before returning to routine batch work, provided doing so will not interrupt a safety-critical repair. Record the sent time and job identifier on the card. If interrupted, leave the card visibly marked 'authorized, not sent'; the sender retains responsibility until the other staff member explicitly accepts it. Check unsent cards at each of the two daily inbox reviews.

An order being sent supports no arrival or pickup promise by itself. Record the supplier's actual status, give a conditional pickup window only when delivery evidence and workshop capacity support it, and disclose delays promptly. If information or authorization is incomplete, resolve it before ordering and communicate that timing remains unconfirmed.

This uses the existing contact moment, two staff, job cards and inbox. It may save an entire supplier cycle for some jobs, but benefits depend on supplier operations and genuine batching delays. Compared with twice-daily order sending, it adds interruptions and may offer no gain where dispatch is infrequent or parts are backordered.
EXPAND.experiment:
The staff member sending orders owns a four-week trial. Where the initial review supports the mechanism, alternate eligible authorized jobs between immediate release and current batch release; do not delay urgent work solely for comparison. Both groups use the same evidence requirements for estimates and disclose delays.

Record authorization-to-order time, order-to-dispatch time and whether a documented dispatch opportunity was caught. Compare missed original pickup estimates, inbound customer status calls and total staff minutes, including interruptions and any correction work. Track estimate availability, pickup lead time and jobs still open after four weeks.

Inspect the first five immediate orders against their sent emails and supplier replies. Stop interrupt-driven sending if it causes an ordering error or repeatedly interrupts repairs without catching an earlier documented dispatch opportunity; return to the ordinary batch process and clear all pending authorized orders. Four weeks may establish only whether avoidable release delay exists, particularly if supplier cutoff evidence is sparse.
